case_study_insert.main_stem: Brightpath Homecare (BHC) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, providing domiciliary care visits with a workforce of 95. Founded in 2007 by Samuel Okafor, the business operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. BHC plans to invest $320,000 in a new homecare scheduling app and three electric care vans, financed by $200,000 hire purchase and $120,000 retained profit rather than a bank loan. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $58, and currently produces 10,500 units a year. BHC faces two problems: care-visit cancellations have risen in recent months and carer absenteeism has reached 10%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Visits Report - Q3 2025: BHC delivered 2,650 care visits last quarter with a missed-visit rate of 2.9%, down from 4.6% a year ago. Client complaints fell from 41 to 22 per month. Average response time to a new care request is 2.1 days. A survey of 350 families found that 73% would pay $12 more for app-based visit tracking and 61% choose a provider on carer reliability. A training audit shows 28 of 95 carers have not completed on-the-job training on the new scheduling app; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $820 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans and hire-purchase deals. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.26 to $14.20 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Homecare fuel and protective-equipment input costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, while household spending on homecare grew 5.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: BHC plans to acquire the electric care vans for its $320,000 expansion. Explain two advantages for BHC of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan to fund the $200,000 of vans.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $200,000 cost into manageable instalments and secures the vans immediately, so BHC can start the app-based visit-tracking service without a large lump-sum outflow, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $180,000 a year and the 8.8% input-cost rise.

Point 2: Unlike the bank loan, hire purchase needs no separate collateral and keeps the $120,000 retained profit intact as a buffer for care-visit cancellations. It also preserves Samuel Okafor's control, since no bank covenants restrict how the scheduling app and vans are operated.

Hire purchase also matches the asset's life: the three vans generate visits over several years, so spreading $200,000 aligns payments with the $36 contribution on each of the 10,500 visits. It leaves the $120,000 retained profit available for the $820 carer retraining and for absorbing the 8.8% fuel rise, which matters when missed visits are already rising. Samuel Okafor keeps control because no bank covenant can dictate how the scheduling app is used.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BHC's expansion, financing and cost data.

questions.question_text: BHC is launching its new app-based visit-tracking service. Consider local newspaper advertising, community radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should BHC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: Local papers reach families in BHC's operating area and can show the tracking app, but readership is falling, print is costly for a 95-carer firm funding a $320,000 expansion, and response cannot be measured precisely.

Community radio sponsorship: Radio is inexpensive and suits repeated reassurance about carer reliability, reaching local families quickly. However it is audio-only, cannot demonstrate the app, and its narrow reach may not win the 10,500 visits needed to cover $180,000 of fixed costs.

Social media influencer marketing: Family and caregiver influencers reach exactly the 73% of 350 surveyed families who would pay $12 more for visit tracking and the 61% who judge on carer reliability. Engagement is measurable and national in scope at low cost, though results build gradually and rely on influencer trust.

BHC's 2025 operating profit is $480,000, but a poorly targeted launch still wastes scarce marketing funds; influencer fees can be linked to enquiries and judged against the $36 contribution per visit. Newspapers cannot show the tracking app and radio reaches only a local area, whereas families across the service region can be reached digitally. With 2,650 visits last quarter and a 2.9% missed-visit rate, a measurable campaign is essential to justify the $320,000 expansion.

Recommendation: BHC should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the survey segment, demonstrates the app visually and costs far less than print. Newspaper advertising is rejected as costly and untrackable; community radio is rejected as narrow and unable to show the app, so BHC should add leaflets via existing carers to convert the leads.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to BHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BHC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in BHC's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: BHC's missed visits have risen and carer absenteeism has reached 10%. Explain two benefits for BHC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its carers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites BHC's 95 carers to help design the new scheduling app and visit rounds, raising ownership and job satisfaction in line with Maslow's esteem needs. Carers who shape their own routes are likelier to attend reliably, directly cutting the 10% absenteeism behind rising missed visits.

Point 2: Consulting frontline carers produces practical fixes that push the 2.9% missed-visit rate lower and protect the 10,500-visit target. Greater involvement lifts commitment and reduces turnover, avoiding repeated $820 per employee retraining and keeping the new vans fully used.

Participation suits a flat, 95-carer service where frontline staff see missed visits first; their ideas can improve the app and push the 2.9% missed-visit rate lower, protecting the 73% who value tracking. Higher morale reduces the 10% absenteeism and the $820 retraining cycle, supporting the 42.0% gross margin and the $1,344,000 gross profit. Stable carers also sustain the 61% reliability reputation that underpins client retention.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to BHC's missed visits, absenteeism and output.

questions.question_text: BHC must upskill 28 carers to use the new scheduling app. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should BHC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on BHC's own app is directly relevant, costs no fees and keeps all 28 carers making visits, protecting the 2,650 visits delivered last quarter and the fall in missed visits to 2.9%. Drawbacks are that mentor carers lose visit time, errors may be passed on, and there is no formal certificate.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $820 per employee provides structured digital skills and a recognised certificate for 28 carers, costing $22,960 - modest against the $320,000 expansion. It removes carers from rounds, risking more cancellations, and generic modules may not match BHC's app, so on-site practice would still be needed.

The 28 carers amount to about 29% of the 95-strong workforce, so sending them to college would remove a large share of visit capacity and risk more cancellations while the app is being introduced. On-the-job coaching on the real system keeps all 28 visiting and protects the 2,650-visit quarter. BHC should record competence sign-off for care-quality assurance, and can use the 15.0% operating margin to fund short college modules later if formal certification is ever required.

Decision: BHC should choose on-the-job training first, adding short college modules for lead carers. It is cheaper, app-specific and avoids losing visit capacity while absenteeism is 10%; full off-the-job training is rejected because a $22,960 fee and 28 carers off rounds would worsen missed visits and client complaints, and college sessions can follow once the app is embedded.

Spending $22,960 on one cohort would use a noticeable part of the $320,000 expansion, whereas machine-specific coaching can be repeated as new carers join at no extra fee.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in BHC's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in BHC's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and app relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BHC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($58 − $22) = $180,000 ÷ $36 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 care visits a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $58 − $22 = $36. Answer: contribution per unit is $36.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BHC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 5,000-visit break-even point with 10,500 actual visits, a margin of safety of 5,500, to judge whether the new vans and app are busy enough.
2. Use $36 contribution to test a $8 discount to $50, leaving $28 per visit, still above the $22 variable cost while winning back clients lost to cancellations.
3. Set visit targets that cover the $200,000 hire-purchase instalments and justify the $320,000 expansion before Samuel Okafor commits further capital.
4. Track average total cost of $39.14 ($180,000 ÷ 10,500 + $22) each quarter to detect missed-visit waste and to check whether the 8.8% input-cost rise is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 visits | (ii) Contribution per unit = $36 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety vs 10,500 visits; discount modelling vs $180,000 fixed costs; hire-purchase affordability for the $320,000 expansion; and average total cost of $39.14 to monitor input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid, contextual use in (iii) (max 4).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BHC's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BHC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 17.5%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,120,000 on revenue of $2,800,000 is 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,344,000 on revenue of $3,200,000 is 42.0%. Operating profit of $336,000 in 2024 equals 12.0% of revenue and 17.5% of the $1,920,000 capital employed; in 2025 operating profit of $480,000 is 15.0% of revenue and 20.0% of the $2,400,000 capital employed. Cost of sales rose from $1,680,000 to $1,856,000 but more slowly than revenue.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. Gross margins widened from 40.0% to 42.0%, reflecting better control of care-delivery costs; operating margins rose from 12.0% to 15.0%, so more of each visit fee becomes operating profit; and returns on capital employed increased from 17.5% to 20.0%, showing the enlarged van and app asset base remains productive. Interest payable rose from $30,000 to $36,000, a small but growing burden, and an 8.8% fuel-cost rise could erode the gross-margin gain.

Interest payable of $36,000 is small beside $480,000 operating profit, so hire-purchase financing costs do not erase the gain, though the 8.8% input-cost rise should be monitored to defend the 42.0% margin.

Conclusion: BHC's financial position has improved on every permitted measure, and because margins and capital returns both rose the gain is not merely a revenue effect. The main risk is rising hire-purchase interest and input costs, so management should defend the 42.0% gross margin before the $320,000 expansion loads more capital into the business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of margin, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BHC of offering the $12 app-based visit-tracking premium identified in its family survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Of 350 families surveyed, 73% would pay $12 more for app-based tracking and 61% choose on carer reliability, so the premium lifts revenue per visit and protects the $36 contribution even as fuel and equipment costs rise 8.8%. It also supports the new scheduling app's differentiating promise.

Disadvantage: Cost-conscious families may reject the $12 premium, cutting the 10,500 visits required to justify the $320,000 vans and app and worsening the rise in care-visit cancellations. If the app fails or carers resist it, the 2.9% missed-visit rate and 10% absenteeism could worsen, undermining reliability.

BHC should pilot the $12 tracking premium with a subset of the 350 families and compare retention, because the 61% reliability effect depends on the app working flawlessly. A premium could be seen as charging vulnerable clients, so some revenue should fund faster response to the 2.1-day care-request time and the $820 training. That reinvestment protects the 42.0% gross margin and the 10,500-visit base that services the $200,000 hire-purchase commitments.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to BHC's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in homecare input costs will affect BHC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): BHC uses $200,000 hire purchase rather than a bank loan, so the 0.75 percentage-point rise may lift hire-purchase charges; as an illustrative bound only, 0.0075 × $200,000 = $1,500 a year if fully passed on, small beside $180,000 of fixed costs. It also raises the cost of any future borrowing, which BHC can limit by negotiating a fixed deal.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.20 an hour): With a workforce of 95, many care visits are delivered by hourly-paid carers, so this lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or pay rates, so no annual total can be invented; the sound test is productivity - 10,500 visits ÷ 95 carers = about 110.5 visits per worker - meaning the rise is absorbable only if that productivity holds, or the $36 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (8.8%): The $22 variable cost per visit covers fuel and protective equipment, but the insert does not split it, so only a bound is honest: a full 8.8% rise is 0.088 × $22 = $1.94 per visit, or about $20,300 a year at 10,500 visits (10,500 × $1.94). Even a partial rise cuts contribution, and the $12 premium offsets only part.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in homecare input costs has the greatest impact because it applies to all 10,500 visits and directly erodes the $36 contribution funding the $320,000 expansion; the wage rise is serious but manageable at about 110.5 visits per carer, and the interest rise costs at most $1,500 and can be fixed, so neither matches the input-cost shock.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to BHC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on BHC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in BHC's context with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
